steps.user_message: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm single in Austin TX. W-2 from Pacific Software: $96,500. Additional income: $18,400 (freelance writing, 5 clients), $2,100 from Capital One 360, $420 from Schwab. Home office: 120 sq ft exclusive; I pay $1,750/month for 720 sq ft. Deductions: $3,200 student loan interest (Nelnet, 2018–2021); $1,500 to Salvation Army have the receipt; $540 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, and what forms I need?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Here’s how your 2024 return likely shakes out and what you’ll need.

What you can deduct
- Standard deduction vs itemizing
  - 2024 standard deduction (single): $14,600.
  - Your likely itemized deductions look low (e.g., $1,500 charity; no mortgage interest; Texas has no state income tax, and rent isn’t deductible). Unless you have large medical expenses or significant sales tax on big purchases, you’ll almost certainly take the standard deduction.
- Student loan interest ($3,200 listed)
  - Max deductible is $2,500, but it phases out for single filers as MAGI approaches the mid-$90k range. With your income, this deduction will be fully phased out ($0).
- Charitable contributions ($1,500 to Salvation Army)
  - Deductible only if you itemize. Since you’ll likely take the standard deduction, this won’t reduce your tax.
- Unreimbursed employee expenses ($540)
  - Not deductible for W‑2 employees in 2024 (TCJA suspension). If these are related to your freelance work, they can be deducted on Schedule C instead.
- Home office (120 sq ft, exclusive use; 720 sq ft home; rent $1,750/mo)
  - You qualify for the deduction (exclusive and regular use for your writing business).
  - Methods:
    - Simplified: 120 sq ft x $5 = $600.
    - Actual: allocate rent by business-use percentage: 120/720 = 16.67%. Annual rent $21,000 x 16.67% ≈ $3,500. This is usually better for you. You can also include a business share of utilities/renter’s insurance if applicable.
  - Limit: It can’t create/increase a Schedule C loss; any unused amount can carry forward (actual method).

Self-employment tax and related deductions
- Net profit estimate (writing): $18,400 − $3,500 home office ≈ $14,900 (before any other business expenses).
- Self-employment tax: about 15.3% of 92.35% of net ≈ $2,104.
- Above-the-line deduction: You can deduct half of SE tax ≈ $1,052 on Form 1040.
- QBI deduction: Likely 20% of qualified business income; rough ballpark ≈ $2,700–$2,800 given your numbers (final figure depends on your exact net and adjustments). Claimed on Form 8995.

How to report your income
- W‑2: $96,500 (Form W‑2).
- Interest: $2,100 from Capital One 360 (Form 1099‑INT). Because your total interest exceeds $1,500, you’ll file Schedule B.
- Schwab $420: If dividends (1099‑DIV), they go on Schedule B and possibly qualified dividend rates apply; if interest (1099‑INT), include with interest. Keep both forms as applicable.
- Freelance $18,400 from 5 clients: Report all income on Schedule C (you should receive 1099‑NEC from clients who paid ≥$600, but report all income whether or not you got a form).

Forms you’ll likely need to file
- Form 1040
- Schedule 1 (additional income/adjustments; Schedule C flows here; also where the SE tax half-deduction shows)
- Schedule B (interest/dividends; required since interest > $1,500)
- Schedule C (freelance income and expenses)
- Schedule SE (self-employment tax)
- Form 8829 (home office using actual expenses). If you use the simplified method, you won’t file 8829—just a worksheet with Schedule C.
- Form 8995 (QBI deduction)
- No state income tax return for Texas

Recommended next steps / clarifications
- Confirm whether the $420 from Schwab is interest or dividends (and whether any are qualified dividends).
- Confirm whether the $540 unreimbursed expenses are for your W‑2 job (not deductible) or your freelance business (deduct on Schedule C).
- Gather any additional business expenses (internet, a business share of utilities/renter’s insurance, supplies, software, professional fees, etc.) to reduce Schedule C profit.
- Make sure you have: W‑2, any 1099‑NEC, 1099‑INT, 1099‑DIV, and (if applicable) 1098‑E (student loan interest—though you’re phased out).
- Consider 2025 quarterly estimated taxes (Form 1040‑ES) due to your freelance income.

If you want, I can run the numbers more precisely once you confirm the Schwab income type and any additional business expenses (internet, utilities, renter’s insurance, supplies, etc.).
